newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Former NZ Social Credit leader Bruce Beetham dies.
newsitem.headline: Former NZ Social Credit leader Bruce Beetham dies.

text.p: WELLINGTON, May 4 - Former MP and Social Credit leader Bruce Beetham died on Saturday.
NZPA reports Beetham, 61, died suddenly at Palmerston North Hospital at 9.30 p.m. He had suffered in the past from a heart condition.
Beetham had been in hospital for nearly two weeks recovering from an angina attack.
Born in New Plymouth on February 16, 1936, he trained as a secondary school teacher and worked in New Plymouth, Taupo and Piopio before becoming a lecturer at Hamilton Teachers' College.
He burst on to the New Zealand political scene in 1972 when he was catapulted into the leadership of the then Social Credit Political League.
For the next 12 years he was one of the country's most prominent politicians.
During that period he brought Social Credit out of the political wilderness, worked to shed the league's "funny money" image and elevated it to creditable third party status.
In a by-election in 1978 Beetham took Rangitikei from National's Les Gandar to become the first Social Credit MP since Vern Cracknell some 15 years previously.
In 1981 he was returned as Rangitikei MP and under his leadership Social Credit gained more than 20 percent of the vote that year.

Although defeated in Rangitikei in 1984, Beetham retained the Social Credit leadership until 1986, when the league became the Democratic Party (now part of the Alliance) and changed its financial direction.
Two years later he formed and lead Social Credit New Zealand -- not a political party but an organisation dedicated to furthering Social Credit aims and financial principles.
He was chairman of SCNZ from 1991 to 1995.
Beetham stood for election as a Democrat in 1987 and Social Creditor in 1990 before "retiring" from active national politics to devote himself to local authority affairs.

Mayor of Hamilton from 1976-77 before he entered Parliament, he served as a Marton Borough councillor and deputy mayor from 1986 to 1989, represented Rangitikei on the Wanganui Hospital Board and then the Manawatu-Wanganui Area Health Board from 1986 to 1991 and was the Rangitikei representative on the Manawatu-Wanganui Regional Council since 1989.
He was the chairman of that council's resource management committee and senior resource consents commissioner.

Beetham was also a member of the Massey University Council, chairman of the board of the Palmerston North College of Education and an executive member of the New Zealand Council for Teacher Education.
He was awarded the Queen's Service Order in 1988 for public services to New Zealand, and the 1990 commemorative medal.
Beetham is survived by his wife, Beverley, four children and two stepsons.
His funeral service will be held at St Stephen's Anglican Church in Marton at 11.30 a.m. on Wednesday.
Democrats leader and Alliance MP John Wright, who worked with Beetham on the Social Credit executive from 1979 to 1986, described the former MP as a man of "tremendous talent".
"He did a marvellous job for the party in the House at a very tough time for third parties," Wright said.
Beetham campaigned during his time in Parliament for many of the rights and funding that third parties now enjoyed.
Alliance leader Jim Anderton said Beetham played a unique role in the development of the Social Credit party at a critical time.
"Although towards the end of his career he seemed to get lost in the political wilderness, the leadership role he exerted cannot be taken away."
Beetham was also an early advocate of proportional representation, Anderton said. He extended his sympathy to Mr Beetham's wife and family.
Labour leader Helen Clark said Beetham's achievement in winning the Rangitikei seat was remarkable.
"Mr Beetham had for several decades stood firmly for the political beliefs that drove the Social Credit movement.
"For a time under his leadership, the Social Credit vote soared to over 20 percent, a considerable achievement for which he should receive full credit," Clark said.
